passage:
Bidisha, you think this pimple is the end of the world? Come, sit near Didu.
When I was fifteen, just plain Lakshmi in Class 9, my father had the tailor stitch me a school bag from an old grain sack. Green, with a big red patch. Everyone else had shiny ones from Calcutta. I was sure the whole school was staring at that patch. I stopped going to the annual function, I skipped the science fair, I even pushed the bag under my desk before the first bell.
Then one day my best friend Mala borrowed it. She carried it around all day. Afterwards I asked, "Did anyone laugh?" She said, "Nobody even looked. They were all busy fixing their own plaits."
Three functions I missed, for a patch nobody saw.

qa.q: What colour was the patch on Lakshmi's bag?
qa.a: It was a big red patch on a green bag.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi push the bag under her desk before the first bell?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and sure every eye was fixed on that red patch, so hiding it seemed the only way to escape being judged.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lakshmi, and why did it work?
qa.a: Letting Mala carry the bag for a day tested the fear against reality, and Mala's report that nobody looked showed how small the audience really was.

qa.q: How might Bidisha hear Didu's story about the three missed functions?
qa.a: Bidisha may start to wonder whether the pimple is as noticeable as it feels, and whether skipping things would be the real loss.

grounding: A grandmother recalls hiding an odd school bag and skipping events, sure everyone stared, until a friend's test showed no one noticed.

passage:
The school bus to the inter-school quiz in Gangtok left at 7:40, and at 7:32 Ira was still in front of the bathroom mirror, pressing a cold spoon to the red bump on her chin. It had grown overnight. She had already skipped the class photo last week for the same reason. The rain meant hood up on the way, but inside the hall hoods would come off.
"I'm not going," she told Pema on the phone. "Everyone will stare at my face for three hours."
"Ira, we're a team of three. They'll stare at the buzzer."
Ira went, chin tucked into her collar. In the first round she was sure the judges were looking at her chin. By round three she had answered four questions, and Pema was hugging her.
Nobody mentioned the pimple once.

qa.q: What time did the school bus to the quiz leave?
qa.a: The school bus left at 7:40.

qa.q: Why was Ira sure everyone would stare at her face for three hours?
qa.a: Ira felt self-conscious because the bump looked enormous to her in the mirror, so she assumed it would look just as huge to everyone in the hall. 😰

qa.q: What was the turning point that got Ira to the quiz?
qa.a: Pema reminded her they were a team and people would watch the buzzer, which let her choose to go despite the fear.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt if Ira had skipped the quiz?
qa.a: Pema would have been let down and a teammate short, and might never have guessed that a pimple was the reason.

grounding: A teen with a new pimple nearly skips a quiz, sure everyone will stare, yet nobody mentions it.

passage:
In the lift of their Andheri building, Saurabh held his new backpack behind his legs. His father had bought it at the Saturday market: stiff brown canvas, a zip that squeaked. Everyone in Class 9 had sleek black ones.
"You coming to the science exhibition tomorrow?" Chetan asked.
"Fever," Saurabh said, though he had none. He pictured the whole corridor turning to look at the brown bag, the squeaky zip, the market price practically printed on it.
Chetan shrugged. "Bring any bag. I need you on the volcano model."
That night Saurabh tried to count how many times anyone had said something about his bag in two weeks. He could remember only one, and it was Chetan asking if it had a bottle pocket.

qa.q: Where had Saurabh's father bought the backpack?
qa.a: His father had bought it at the Saturday market.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh claim a fever to skip the exhibition?
qa.a: He pictured the whole corridor turning to stare at the brown bag and judging him, and staying away felt safer than being seen.

qa.q: What choice that night gave Saurabh a more realistic picture?
qa.a: Counting the real comments from two weeks showed him there was just one, and a harmless one, so he could rethink skipping.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Saurabh's bag?
qa.a: To Chetan it's just a bag, maybe one with a handy bottle pocket; Chetan cares far more about Saurabh's help on the volcano model. 🙂

grounding: A teenage boy dodges a school exhibition over a plain market bag, though only one person ever mentioned it.

passage:
Karthik called at seven. "Where are you? The farewell's started."
"I'm not coming," Asif said.
"What? You helped plan the whole thing!"
"Did you see my haircut? The barber ruined it. There's literally a gap on one side."
"So?"
"So everyone will stare. There'll be photos. It'll be in everyone's phone forever."
"Asif, nobody's looking at your head. Half the class is freaking out about their own outfits. Hema's crying because her dupatta ripped."
"That's different."
"How?"
"It's… mine."
Karthik laughed, not unkindly. "Wear a cap. Or don't. Honestly, if you don't come, people will notice that more than any haircut."
Asif touched the side of his head, then looked at his kurta hanging on the door. "Give me twenty minutes."
When he arrived, three people said hi. Not one mentioned his hair.

qa.q: What was wrong with Asif's haircut, according to Asif?
qa.a: There's literally a gap on one side.

qa.q: How did Asif feel about his haircut, and why?
qa.a: Asif felt self-conscious and anxious, sure that everyone would stare at the gap and that it would be in everyone's phone forever.

qa.q: What did Karthik say that turned Asif's decision around?
qa.a: Karthik pointed out that the others were busy worrying about their own outfits, and that people would notice Asif missing more than any haircut.

qa.q: How might Karthik see Asif's worry?
qa.a: Karthik finds it a little funny but cares, knowing Asif helped plan the farewell and wants him there.

grounding: It shows a teenager sure everyone will stare at a bad haircut and nearly skipping a farewell, when the audience is far smaller than imagined.

passage:
Last year, in Class 10, I skipped sports day because of a school bag. I'm Kamal, and I know how that sounds.
My old bag had torn, so Appa gave me his old office bag, brown and stiff with a big buckle. "A proper bag for my son," he said proudly. The first day I carried it, I was sure the whole school was staring. On the stairs I held it behind my legs. I imagined people laughing about it at lunch.
When sports day came, you had to carry your things to the ground. I told Amma I had a stomach ache. I stayed home.
Rukmini, my cousin, who's in my class, told me later that nobody had mentioned my bag at all. "Half of them were worrying about their own shoes," she said.
Now I look at that bag and feel a bit silly. The only person who stared at it all year was me.

qa.q: What did Appa give Kamal when his old bag tore?
qa.a: Appa gave him his old office bag, brown and stiff with a big buckle.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel so sure the whole school was staring at the bag?
qa.a: Feeling embarrassed about it made the bag seem huge to him, so he imagined everyone noticing and laughing, though no one mentioned it.

qa.q: What choice did Kamal make that he now regrets, and what might he try instead next time?
qa.a: He skipped sports day, claiming a stomach ache; next time he could go and see for himself whether people really notice.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see the whole bag worry?
qa.a: Rukmini seems to find it a bit surprising, since nobody talked about the bag and most classmates were worried about their own shoes.

grounding: A teenager recalls skipping a school event because he was sure everyone judged his old bag, when the audience was far smaller than imagined.

passage: In Class 9, my father couldn't afford a new school bag, so I carried my cousin's old one: bright orange, with a cartoon duck on the front. I was sure the whole school stared at it. I walked with it held behind my back. I skipped the inter-school science fair, which I had wanted to go to for months, because we'd have to carry our bags on the bus and I imagined forty people seeing the duck. Mahima, my lab partner, went and came back with a medal. Years later I asked her if she remembered my orange bag. She thought hard. "You had an orange bag?" That was it. The duck I had hidden for a whole year, the reason I missed the fair, nobody had noticed. I still think about that. Arnab and the invisible duck.

qa.q: What was on the front of the old bag?
qa.a: A cartoon duck.

qa.q: Why did Arnab skip the science fair?
qa.a: Arnab felt anxious and embarrassed, sure forty people would stare at the orange duck bag on the bus.

qa.q: What would you tell Arnab back in Class 9?
qa.a: That people notice far less than it feels, like Mahima who never saw the bag, so don't let a bag keep you from the fair.

qa.q: What does Mahima's answer years later show?
qa.a: Mahima didn't remember the bag at all, showing that the staring audience Arnab feared barely existed.

grounding: A teenager recalls hiding an old bag and missing a science fair, sure everyone stared, though nobody had noticed.

passage:
Class teacher's note, sports week, Class 9C
Harsha has asked to be excused from the relay on Saturday. When I asked why, she said her new glasses are "thick and ugly" and that "everyone will stare when I run." She has also stopped sitting in the front row since getting them last week. I asked Jyoti, who sits with her, whether anyone had said anything. Jyoti looked surprised: "She has new glasses?" I spoke with Harsha at lunch and told her, gently, what Jyoti had said. She laughed a little, then asked if she could wear a sports band to keep them steady. I have arranged one from the sports room. She is back on the relay list, and I will see how she settles next week.

qa.q: When did Harsha get the new glasses?
qa.a: Last week.

qa.q: Why did Harsha ask to be excused from the relay?
qa.a: She felt anxious and self-conscious, sure everyone would stare at her new glasses when she ran.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Harsha?
qa.a: Checked with Jyoti, gently shared that Jyoti hadn't even noticed, and arranged a sports band, so Harsha felt able to run.

qa.q: How does Jyoti's reaction show the real audience?
qa.a: Jyoti, who sits with Harsha, didn't even know about the new glasses, so hardly anyone was staring.

grounding: A teacher records a teenage girl avoiding the relay, sure everyone stares at her new glasses, when even her deskmate hadn't noticed.

passage:
Thursday.
Woke up with a huge pimple on the tip of my nose. The farewell party is tomorrow. I'm Nitin, and I'm the boy who was supposed to give the vote of thanks. Now I'm not going. Everyone will stare at it the whole time. I'll be "pimple nose" in every photo.
Friday.
Told Ma I had a headache. Stayed home. Lavanya from my class sent photos of the party. Everyone looked happy. Nobody asked where I was, except Lavanya, who said, "The vote of thanks was so boring without you."
I looked at the photos properly. Three boys had pimples. One girl had a plaster on her chin. I hadn't even noticed them until now.
Missed my own farewell for a spot no one would have seen.

qa.q: How many boys in the photos had pimples?
qa.a: Three boys had pimples.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling on Thursday?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious, sure everyone would stare at the pimple and call him "pimple nose" in every photo.

qa.q: What could Nitin try the next time he worries about his looks before an event?
qa.a: Ask how much he notices other people's spots, as he did with the photos, and go anyway, since the audience is smaller than he imagines.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Nitin missing the party?
qa.a: Lavanya missed him and found the vote of thanks boring without him, and likely wouldn't have noticed the pimple.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him skipping his farewell because of a pimple, sure everyone would stare, then seeing others' spots he hadn't noticed.

passage: In Malerkotla, the annual day dance was on Saturday, and Rehana had the lead position in the front row. Then her new suit didn't come from the tailor in time, and Ammi said she'd have to wear her elder cousin's old green one, faded at the sleeves. Rehana looked at herself in the mirror and felt sick. Everyone would see the faded sleeves. The whole school, all the parents. She told the dance teacher she had a sprained ankle. Afreen, dancing behind her in the second row, came over on Friday evening. "Your ankle is fine. I saw you run for the bus." Rehana showed her the sleeves. Afreen squinted. "I can't even see it. From the audience, it'll be a green blur." Then she added, "And everyone will be watching their own daughters anyway." Rehana laughed despite herself. She told the teacher her ankle was better.

passage:
Yuki saw it in the bathroom mirror at 6:40: a red bump on the side of her nose, shiny and enormous.
The school sports day in Lyon was that afternoon, with class photos on the front steps. Yuki texted Beatriz: I'm sick. Not coming.
Then she spent the morning in her room imagining the photo: thirty smiling faces and one nose, framed in the school corridor for years. She pictured the boys in the back row nudging each other.
At four, Beatriz sent the photo. "You missed it!! Look at my hair, the wind destroyed me 😩"
Yuki zoomed in. Beatriz's fringe stood straight up. Two people had their eyes closed. Someone's shirt was inside out.
Yuki hadn't noticed any of it until she looked for it. Nobody had been looking for her nose either, she thought slowly, and put the phone down.

qa.q: At what time did Yuki see the bump in the mirror?
qa.a: Yuki saw it in the bathroom mirror at 6:40.

qa.q: Why did skipping sports day feel necessary to Yuki?
qa.a: Yuki felt embarrassed and anxious, sure that thirty classmates would stare at the red bump in a photo framed for years.

qa.q: What could Yuki try next time a pimple makes her want to hide?
qa.a: Yuki could go anyway and remember the photo, where everyone was busy with their own hair and eyes, not hunting for flaws.

qa.q: How did Beatriz experience the class photo?
qa.a: Beatriz was busy worrying about a wind-blown fringe, not studying anyone else's face.

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping a school event over a pimple, sure everyone will stare, while the others are focused on themselves.

Keerthana's school bag had torn on Monday, so she carried her cousin's old one: brown, square, with a cartoon duck faded on the flap.
By Wednesday she had stopped going to the canteen. She kept the bag under her desk, pushed back with her feet. When the class teacher announced Annual Day dance practice in the hall, Keerthana asked to stay back with a "headache".
"You're in my group," Ishita said at the door. "We need you for the formation."
"I'll come next week."
"Why?"
Keerthana's face heated. "The bag. Everyone's been laughing at the duck."
Ishita blinked at it. "That's a duck? I thought it was a stain." She shrugged. "Nobody's looked, Keerthu. Half the class is crying about the steps. Come."
Keerthana looked at the bag, then at the door, and followed.

qa.q: What was faded on the flap of the old bag?
qa.a: A cartoon duck was faded on the flap.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling about the bag?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and exposed, convinced everyone was laughing at the duck, so she hid from the canteen and dance practice.

qa.q: What could Keerthana try the next time she wants to skip an event over her looks?
qa.a: Keerthana could check the fear with one friend first, as Ishita showed her, before deciding to stay away.

qa.q: How does Ishita see the bag?
qa.a: Ishita had barely noticed it, even mistaking the duck for a stain, and is more worried about the dance formation.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding school events over an unfashionable bag she thinks everyone judges, when hardly anyone noticed.

passage:
Hi Anirban,
Thanks for the photos from your hostel. Mine are fewer, because I skipped the school fete. Don't laugh.
It's the new glasses. The frame is huge and brown, the only one Ma could get fitted in a day after I sat on my old pair. I was sure every single person would stare. I even practised answers in my head for when they asked.
So I stayed home and watched the fete on the class group from my bed.
Here's the embarrassing bit. On Monday I wore them to school. One person, one, said "New specs?" and then asked me for the maths homework. That was it. Nobody else even blinked.
I missed the fete, the dunk tank and the dance, all for an audience of one person who cared more about homework.
Next time, remind me of this letter.
Trisha

qa.q: How many people said anything about the glasses on Monday?
qa.a: One person said 'New specs?' and then asked for the maths homework.

qa.q: Why did Trisha practise answers before the fete?
qa.a: Trisha was anxious and self-conscious, sure every single person would stare at the huge brown frame and ask about it.

qa.q: What could Trisha do next time a new look brings the urge to skip an event?
qa.a: Trisha could go for a short while and count the real reactions, as happened on Monday, instead of trusting the imagined crowd.

qa.q: What might Anirban think when reading the letter?
qa.a: Anirban might smile at the story and feel fond of Trisha, and might remind Trisha of it next time, as asked.

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping a school fete over new glasses, sure everyone would stare, and finding the real audience was one person.

passage: Okay, Pranav, I'll tell you why I didn't come to the Diwali mela at school. Promise not to laugh. That morning I woke up with a huge red pimple right on my nose. Huge.
